search-in-a-binary-search-tree.pattern: BST descent: compare and go left or right (binary search on a tree)

approaches.name: Search the whole tree
approaches.idea: Ignore the ordering and look at every node with a DFS until one has value `val`.
steps: If `root` is null or holds `val`, return it.
Search the left subtree; if found, return that node.
Otherwise return the result of searching the right subtree.
approaches.why: It may visit all n nodes; the stack is as deep as the tree.

approaches.name: Walk down using the BST order
approaches.idea: At each node the ordering tells you which side `val` must be on, so follow a single path from the root.
steps: Start at `root`.
While the node is not null and its value is not `val`: go left if `val` is smaller, right otherwise.
Return the node (null if the walk fell off the tree).
approaches.why: One root-to-leaf path at most: O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a chain. The loop needs no stack.

convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.pattern: Divide and conquer: the middle element is the root

approaches.name: Recursively take the middle as the root
approaches.idea: Making the middle element the root puts (almost) the same number of values on each side; doing the same for each half keeps every subtree balanced, and the sorted order makes it a BST.
steps: `build(lo, hi)`: if `lo > hi`, return null.
Take `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` as the root.
Set `root.left = build(lo, mid − 1)` and `root.right = build(mid + 1, hi)`; return `root`.
approaches.why: Each value becomes one node. The recursion depth is the height of the balanced tree, log n (the output tree itself aside). A simpler alternative — inserting the values one by one — would build a chain, since they arrive in sorted order.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.pattern: BST split point: the first node whose value lies between p and q

approaches.name: Generic binary-tree LCA
approaches.idea: Ignore the BST order and use the general method: a node whose left and right subtrees each contain one of the targets (or which is a target) is the answer.
steps: If `root` is null, `p` or `q`, return `root`.
Recurse into both subtrees.
If both return a node, return `root`; otherwise return whichever is non-null.
approaches.why: It may visit every node, because it never uses the values to choose a side.

approaches.name: Walk down until p and q split
approaches.idea: If both values are smaller than the current node, both targets are in its left subtree, so the LCA is too; if both are larger, go right. Otherwise the node lies between them (or equals one), so it is the LCA.
steps: Start at `root`.
If `p.val` and `q.val` are both less than the node's value, move left; if both greater, move right.
Otherwise return the current node.
approaches.why: A single downward path with no recursion: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a chain.

validate-binary-search-tree.pattern: DFS with a valid (low, high) range per node, or an inorder walk that must strictly increase

approaches.name: Compare every node with its whole subtrees
approaches.idea: Apply the definition directly: at every node, check that the maximum of its left subtree is smaller and the minimum of its right subtree is larger, recomputing those with full subtree scans.
steps: For a node, compute `max(left subtree)` and `min(right subtree)` by visiting those subtrees.
Fail if `max(left) >= node.val` or `min(right) <= node.val`.
Check both subtrees the same way.
approaches.why: Every node rescans its subtrees, so each node is visited once per ancestor: O(n·h), which is O(n²) for a chain.

approaches.name: Inorder into a list, check it strictly increases
approaches.idea: An inorder traversal of a BST lists its values in sorted order. Collect them and check every value is larger than the one before.
steps: Collect the values with an inorder traversal (left, node, right).
Return false if any `vals[i] <= vals[i − 1]`; otherwise true.
approaches.why: One traversal and one scan; the list holds all n values.

approaches.name: DFS with value bounds
approaches.idea: Every node must lie strictly inside a range set by its ancestors: going left lowers the upper bound to the parent's value, going right raises the lower bound. Checking each node against its range checks the whole definition.
steps: `valid(node, low, high)`: true for null.
If `node.val <= low` or `node.val >= high`, return false.
Return `valid(left, low, node.val) && valid(right, node.val, high)`.
Start with bounds −∞ and +∞ (64-bit, or null), since values reach ±2³¹.
approaches.why: Each node is checked once against two numbers. Comparing only with the parent is the classic bug: `[5,4,6,null,null,3,7]` passes a parent check but 3 is in 5's right subtree.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.pattern: Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order (stop at the k-th)

approaches.name: Collect all values and sort
approaches.idea: Ignore the BST property: gather every value, sort, and take index `k − 1`.
steps: Collect all values with any traversal.
Sort them and return the one at index `k − 1`.
approaches.why: The sort dominates; the list holds n values.

approaches.name: Full inorder traversal
approaches.idea: Inorder visits a BST in sorted order, so the list it produces needs no sorting.
steps: Collect values with an inorder traversal (left, node, right).
Return `vals[k − 1]`.
approaches.why: It still walks the whole tree and stores every value even when k is small.

approaches.name: Iterative inorder that stops at the k-th node
approaches.idea: Run inorder with an explicit stack and count nodes as they are visited; stop the moment the k-th is reached.
steps: Push the path down the left spine onto a stack.
Pop a node: it is the next smallest. Decrease `k`; if it hits 0, return the value.
Move to the popped node's right child and push its left spine; repeat.
approaches.why: It walks down to the minimum (h steps) and then visits only k nodes. The stack never holds more than one root-to-leaf path. (If the tree changed often, storing subtree sizes in each node would allow O(h) queries.)

insert-into-a-binary-search-tree.pattern: BST descent to the empty spot where the value belongs

approaches.name: Recursive insert
approaches.idea: A new value always becomes a leaf. Follow the BST order down; the first null child on that path is where it goes.
steps: If `root` is null, return a new node with `val`.
If `val < root.val`, set `root.left = insert(root.left, val)`; otherwise `root.right = insert(root.right, val)`.
Return `root`.
approaches.why: One root-to-leaf path; the recursion uses a stack frame per level.

approaches.name: Iterative insert
approaches.idea: The same walk with a loop: move down until the side you need is empty, then attach the new node there.
steps: If `root` is null, return a new node.
From `root`, go left if `val` is smaller, right otherwise; when that child is null, attach the new node there and stop.
Return `root`.
approaches.why: The same path as the recursive version, with constant extra memory.

delete-node-in-a-bst.pattern: BST delete: replace a two-child node by its inorder successor

approaches.name: Rebuild the tree without the key
approaches.idea: Read all values in sorted order (inorder), drop `key`, and build a fresh balanced BST from what is left.
steps: Collect the values with an inorder traversal, skipping `key`.
Build a balanced BST from the sorted list by taking the middle as the root recursively.
Return the new root.
approaches.why: Every node is read and rebuilt, even though deleting one value only needs to touch a single path.

approaches.name: Find the node and splice it out
approaches.idea: Search for `key` using the BST order. A node with at most one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children takes the value of its inorder successor (the smallest value in its right subtree), and that successor is then deleted from the right subtree.
steps: If `root` is null, return null. If `key < root.val`, delete from the left subtree; if greater, from the right.
Found it: if it has no left child, return its right child; if no right child, return its left child.
Two children: find the leftmost node of the right subtree, copy its value into `root`, and delete that value from the right subtree.
Return `root`.
approaches.why: The search and the successor's removal each follow one downward path. The successor has no left child, so removing it is the simple case.

binary-search-tree-iterator.pattern: Controlled inorder traversal with an explicit stack (left spine)

approaches.name: Flatten the tree up front
approaches.idea: Do a full inorder traversal in the constructor and store the values; `next` and `hasNext` just walk the list.
steps: Constructor: inorder traversal into a list; set an index to 0.
`next()`: return `list[index++]`.
`hasNext()`: return `index < list.size()`.
approaches.why: O(n) work once in the constructor, then O(1) calls — but it stores all n values instead of the O(h) the problem asks for.

approaches.name: Stack of the pending left spine
approaches.idea: Pause an iterative inorder traversal between calls. The stack holds the nodes whose left side is done but which have not been returned yet; the top is always the next smallest.
steps: Constructor: push `root` and all its left descendants.
`next()`: pop the top node; push its right child and that child's left descendants; return the popped value.
`hasNext()`: return whether the stack is non-empty.
approaches.why: Each node is pushed and popped exactly once over the whole iteration, so n calls cost O(n). The stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.

recover-binary-search-tree.pattern: Inorder should be increasing: find the two places it goes down (Morris traversal for O(1) space)

approaches.name: Sort the inorder values and write them back
approaches.idea: Collect the values inorder, sort them, and write them back into the nodes in inorder. Sorted values in inorder positions are exactly a valid BST.
steps: Collect the nodes in inorder.
Sort their values.
Assign the k-th sorted value to the k-th inorder node.
approaches.why: The sort dominates; the node list and value list take O(n). It ignores the fact that only two values are wrong.

approaches.name: Inorder with a previous pointer, find the two misplaced nodes
approaches.idea: In the inorder sequence, a swap creates one or two "drops" where `prev.val > cur.val`. The first misplaced node is `prev` at the first drop; the second is `cur` at the last drop. Swap their values.
steps: Do an inorder traversal keeping `prev`.
At each drop (`prev.val > cur.val`): if `first` is unset, set `first = prev`; always set `second = cur`.
After the traversal, swap `first.val` and `second.val`.
approaches.why: One traversal with O(1) work per node; the recursion stack is h deep. Adjacent swapped nodes give a single drop, which the "always set second" rule still handles.

approaches.name: Morris inorder traversal (no stack)
approaches.idea: Morris traversal walks inorder without recursion or a stack by temporarily linking each node's inorder predecessor back to it, then removing that link on the way back. Run the same drop detection along the way.
steps: Set `cur = root`. If `cur` has no left child, visit it and go right.
Otherwise find its predecessor (rightmost node of the left subtree). If the predecessor's right is null, link it to `cur` and go left.
If the predecessor already links to `cur`, remove the link, visit `cur`, and go right.
"Visit" means the drop check with `prev`; at the end swap `first.val` and `second.val`.
approaches.why: Each edge is walked a constant number of times (predecessor searches add up to O(n) in total), and only a few pointers are used. All temporary links are removed, so the tree shape is restored.
